title: Lecture #30: Iterable Interface in Java
topics: Why the iterator is a separate object

questions.question: In the hierarchy `Object → ? → Collection → List/Queue/Set`, which interface sits directly above `Collection` and declares the `iterator()` method?
options: `Iterator`
`Map`
`Iterable`
`Comparable`
questions.explanation: `Iterable` is the root interface representing any object whose elements can be traversed one by one; its key method is `Iterator<T> iterator()`, and `Collection` extends it. `Iterator` is a different interface — it is the object returned by `iterator()` and provides `hasNext()`/`next()`. Confusing the two names is the classic mistake.

questions.question: Why can't a single loop like `for (int i = 0; i < c.size(); i++) c.get(i)` be used to traverse every kind of `Collection`?
options: Because not every collection is index-based — a Set or Queue has no `get(i)`, so Java needs a common index-free way to traverse: the Iterator
Because `size()` is only available on `List`, not on `Set` or `Queue`
Because index-based loops are slower than iterators for every collection, including ArrayList
Because `get(i)` throws an exception whenever the collection contains duplicates
questions.explanation: Only `List` offers index-based `get(i)`; sets, queues and stacks organise data differently (hashes, trees, LIFO/FIFO). `Iterable`/`Iterator` give every collection one uniform way to visit elements one by one. `size()` is declared in `Collection`, so it exists on all of them, and for an ArrayList an index loop is perfectly fast.

questions.question: You wrote a `NameContainer` class that wraps a `String[]`, and you want callers to write `for (String name : container) { ... }`. What must `NameContainer` do?
options: Extend `ArrayList<String>` so that it becomes index-based
Provide public `hasNext()` and `next()` methods directly on `NameContainer`
Override `toString()` so the loop can split the names
Implement `Iterable<String>` and return an `Iterator<String>` from its `iterator()` method
questions.explanation: The enhanced for loop works on arrays and on any `Iterable`; it calls `iterator()` and then uses `hasNext()`/`next()` on the returned object. That is exactly what Demo2's `NameContainer implements Iterable<String>` does with an anonymous Iterator. Putting `hasNext()`/`next()` on the container itself does not make it usable in a for-each loop.

questions.question: `NameContainer` is the class from the lecture (its iterator returns `names[pos++]` and `hasNext()` is `pos < size`). What does this print?
options: Aditya Rohit Rohan Monu
Rohit Monu
Aditya Rohan
Rohit Monu, followed by an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
questions.explanation: Each `next()` returns the current element and advances `pos`, so every loop pass consumes two names but prints only the second: Rohit (pos becomes 2), then Monu (pos becomes 4). Now `hasNext()` is `4 < 4`, false, so the loop stops cleanly with no exception. With an odd number of names the second `next()` would run past the end, but here there are four.

questions.question: When `for (String name : container) { System.out.println(name); }` runs on an `Iterable`, what does it actually do?
options: It calls `container.get(i)` for `i` from 0 to `size() - 1`
It copies the container into an array first and then loops over the array
It calls `container.iterator()` once, then repeatedly calls `hasNext()` and `next()` on that iterator
It calls `container.iterator()` before every element to fetch the next value
questions.explanation: The enhanced for loop over an Iterable is shorthand for obtaining one iterator and running `while (it.hasNext()) { name = it.next(); ... }`. That is why the commented-out while-loop in Demo2 and the for-each produce the same output. Calling `iterator()` before every element would restart at position 0 each time, and Iterables are not required to have `get(i)`.

questions.question: You loop over an `ArrayList<Integer>` with an `Iterator` and call `list.remove(...)` inside the loop to drop even numbers. It throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. What is the correct fix while still using the iterator?
options: Catch `ConcurrentModificationException` inside the loop and continue
Call `it.remove()` instead of `list.remove(...)` right after `it.next()` returns the even number
Call `it.next()` once more after each `list.remove(...)` to resynchronise the cursor
Mark the loop body `synchronized` so the list cannot change during iteration
questions.explanation: ArrayList's iterator is fail-fast: it remembers the list's modification count and throws when the list is structurally changed behind its back. `Iterator.remove()` removes the last returned element and updates the iterator's own bookkeeping, so iteration continues safely. `synchronized` is about threads — here the same thread modifies the list, so it changes nothing — and catching the exception leaves the iteration broken.

questions.question: The lecture lists methods of `Iterable` and of `Iterator`. Which of these is declared by `Iterable` (not by `Iterator`)?
options: `forEach(...)`
`hasNext()`
`forEachRemaining(...)`
`next()`
questions.explanation: `Iterable` declares `iterator()` plus the default methods `forEach(...)` and `spliterator()`. `Iterator` declares `hasNext()`, `next()`, the default `remove()` and the default `forEachRemaining(...)`. `forEachRemaining` is the tempting distractor because its name looks like `forEach`, but it lives on the Iterator and processes only the elements not yet visited.

questions.topic: Why the iterator is a separate object
questions.question: This `MyArrayList` keeps the cursor inside the list itself instead of in a separate iterator object. What does the nested loop print?
options: All 9 pairs from "10 10" to "30 30"
"10 20" only
questions.explanation: Both loops share the single `pos` field. The outer loop reads 10 (pos=1); the inner loop reads 20 and 30 (pos=3) printing "10 20" and "10 30"; then the outer `hasNext()` sees pos=3 and stops, so 20 and 30 never become `a`. Separate iterator objects (each `iterator()` call returning a fresh cursor) are exactly what fixes this — it is the separation-of-concerns point in the lecture.

questions.question: What is the output of this code (from the lecture's Demo3)?
options: 1, 2, 3 printed on separate lines, then `ConcurrentModificationException`
1, 2, 3, 4, 5 printed on separate lines
1, 2, 4, 5 printed on separate lines
1, 2, 3, 5 printed on separate lines
questions.explanation: `value` is an `int`, so `list.remove(value)` calls `remove(int index)` and removes the element at index 3 (the number 4), not the number 3. Either way the list was structurally modified outside the iterator: 3 is still printed, then `hasNext()` (cursor 3 vs size 4) is true and the next `next()` detects the changed modification count and throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Options that print later elements ignore the fail-fast check.

questions.question: A teammate iterates `[1, 2, 3, 4]` (an `ArrayList<Integer>`) with an Iterator and calls `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(3))` when it sees 3. No exception occurs, so they claim modifying the list inside the loop is safe. What actually happened?
options: ArrayList iterators are not fail-fast, so modifications are always allowed
`remove(Object)` does not change the modification count, so the iterator cannot notice it
After the removal the size became 3, equal to the cursor, so `hasNext()` returned false and the loop ended early — 4 was never visited and the fail-fast check in `next()` never ran
The iterator automatically adjusted its cursor, so 4 was visited normally and the loop finished correctly
questions.explanation: ArrayList's `hasNext()` only compares `cursor != size`; the modification check happens in `next()`. Removing the second-to-last element shrinks size to 3 while cursor is already 3, so the loop silently stops and element 4 is skipped. Fail-fast behaviour is best-effort, not a guarantee — the code is still wrong and should use `it.remove()`.
